blocks.text: On the providence of God concerning sparrows and little birds, in Matth. X, 29. and Luc. XII, 6.

Christ, in Matth. X, 29., says that two sparrows are sold for an assarion, and yet not one of them falls to the ground without God. And in Luc. XII, 6. he says that five sparrows are sold for two assaria, and yet not one of them is forgotten before God. Thus individual sparrows were sold for half an as, or a little less. For those are mistaken who hold that the assarion is half an as. Rather, the assarion is the same as the as. The Latin-Greek Glosses: Asse, Ἀσσάριον [assarion]; read Ἀσσαρίου [assariou]. And elsewhere: Sesquas, Ἓι ἥμισυ ἀσσάριον [hei hēmisy assarion]. Read Ἓν ἥμισυ καὶ ἀσσάριον [hen hēmisy kai assarion]. The Greek-Latin Glosses of Philoxenus: Ἀσσάριον [assarion], Hic as.; Ἀσσαρίου ἥμισυ [assariou hēmisy], Sesquas; read Ἓν ἀσσάριον καὶ ἥμισυ [hen assarion kai hēmisy]. The as, by Budé's reckoning, was worth four of our little deniers and a trifle more. The Syriac translator has ܐܣܪ assar, a word which the Hebrews also often use for the assarion. David Cohen de Lara, in his book De convenientia Rabbinismi [col. 158] cum Graeco, defines אסר assar in Spanish as moneda de tres maravedis, which comes very close to Budé's λογισμὸν [logismon]. In Maimonides' treatise On Shekels, ch. 1. 3.: הסלע ארבעה דינרין והדינר שש מעין ומעה היא היקראת בימי משה רבינו גרה ומאה היא שני פונדיונין ופונדיון שני אסרין ופרוטה אחת משמונה באסר נמצא משקל המעה והיא הגרה שש עשרה שעורות ומשקל האסר ארבע שעורות ומשקל פרוטה חצי שעורה, The shekel is worth four denarii. The denarius six obols. The obol was called a gerah in the days of Moses our master. The obol is worth two [II, 736] pondia, and the pondion two assaria. And the perutah is the eighth part of an assarion. The weight of the obol, which is called a gerah, is sixteen barley grains. The weight of the assarion four grains, of the perutah half a grain. Drusius cites a similar passage from the Book of Commandments. For assarion the Arabic translator has فلس [fals] follis, and for two assaria فلسين [falsayn] two folles; and Jerome has dipondium. But in Matth. V, 26. the same Arabic version has follis for quadrans. And in Marc. XIV, 42. فلسين [falsayn] two folles stands for two mites, that is, two פרוטות perutoth, which together make one quadrans. It is evident, therefore, that this translator, caring little about the true value of the coins, was content to put one cheap coin for another cheap coin, though of different value. And indeed, to be sold for an assarion or an as means nothing other than to be sold off at a low price. For whatever is sold or valued at an as must be cheap. Hence Catullus to his Lesbia:
And the gossip of stern old men, let us value it all at a single as.
Son, you cannot sell it for an as.
You think it not worth an as? O filth, O brothel!

And Cicero, for Quinctius: He says he will not pay an as unless he has first settled all the affairs and accounts of the partnership. And for Roscius the Comedian: Say he gave LLS. CCCIↃↃↃ, he who gave not a single as. And Juvenal, Satire 10:
Whoever still worships Minerva, acquired for a single as.

And the Mishnah at the end of the tractate Chullin, concerning the precept by which the Israelites are commanded to let the mother go when they take eggs and young from a nest, that it may be well with them and their days be prolonged, Deut. XXII, 6. 7.: אם מצוה קלה שהיא באסר אמרה תורה למען ייטב לך והארכת ימים קל וחומר על מצות חמורות שבתורה, If concerning a lighter precept, about a thing that is scarcely worth an assarion, the Law says, “That it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days,” how much more (is the same to be hoped) for the weightier precepts that are in the Law? For assarion the older Greeks would have said obol. Thus in the Birds of Aristophanes the birds complain bitterly of a certain Philocrates, who,
— συνείρων τοὺς σπίνους, πωλεῖ καθ᾽ ἑπτὰ ὀβολοῦ, [syneirōn tous spinous, pōlei kath᾽ hepta obolou,]
